To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the BZR subunit of 52‐53K is phylo‐genetically the most ancient one, that it is the only subunit in the lungfish, that it is still the only subunit present in most of the amphibians, that the subunit patterns of the higher tetrapods are the result of the loss of this ancient subunit and of the evolution of new ones, and that the subunits of the BZR are not homologous with those of the GABA
the 53K band is the only band found in lungfish and most amphibia; that it is the oldest photo‐labelled BZR subunit, and that the BZR of fishes has lost the 53K component.

(a) The BZR subunits of the lungfish and of most amphibians are represented by the 53K band only; (b) the 53K is the oldest subunit; and (c) the evolution of the subunits leads to a progressive reduction of the 53 K band.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of the benzodizapine receptor subunits.
the evolution and the molecular structure of the GABA/benzodiazepine‐receptor‐ionophore complex.
the qualitative evolution of BZR subunits.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the BZR subunit pattern is not a constant entity in evolution and, thus, cannot be considered to be an invariant marker of a given species.
the BZR subunit pattern is phylogenetically highly variable, which is in accordance with its proposed evolutionary late appearance.
the BZR is a relatively late evolutionary development, which is characterized by a qualitative change of the subunits during evolution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the BZR subunit pattern in the brain of the lungfish is the most primitive one, with the exception of the 53‐K subunit.
the subunit patterns of the BZR are phylogenetically more complex than previously thought.
the BZR has evolved from a 53K subunits to a complex subunit pattern in mammals, with the 53K being the oldest and the 53K/51K the most recent addition.
The main takeaway from our work is that
we can use the BZR to study evolutionary changes in the brain.
the subunit pattern of the photo‐affinity‐labeled BZR in the lungfish, the most primitive tetrapod, is the same as that in most of the amphibians.
the benzodiazapine receptor is a relatively new protein in vertebrates.
